entries.response: A function does something when you call it. Write its name, then brackets, then a semicolon — like moveForward();. Nothing happens until you actually call it on its own line.

That's usually a missing bracket or semicolon. Every function call needs both: moveForward(); — brackets even though nothing goes inside them, and a semicolon at the end. Check the line the error message points to first.

Count the cells between the rover and the exit on the grid — that's how many moveForward() calls you need. If it's more than a couple, a loop is worth using instead of writing the same line over and over.

Turning changes which way the rover is facing, not where it is on the grid. moveForward() always moves it one cell in whatever direction it's currently facing — so the order of turns and moves matters.
for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) { moveForward(); } runs moveForward() 6 times. The middle number (6 here) is the one to change — it's how many times the loop repeats.
Check the number in your loop condition against the actual distance to the exit — a loop that says i < 3 only runs 3 times, so if the exit is 4 cells away it'll stop one short.
The Glitch already has working code — the bug is just the number in the loop condition. Check how far the exit actually is versus how many times the loop currently runs.

Check the Error box under the buttons first — a syntax error stops the code running at all. If there's no error and still nothing moves, make sure you've actually replaced the // TODO comment with a real command.
The Hint button under Run and Reset opens this same chat and posts a nudge specific to the construct you're on — one click, no need to type anything.
Reset puts the construct back to its starting code, not just the visuals — so yes, it clears anything you've written. Worth being careful with it if you want to keep what you've got.
Walls, debris, and the edge of the grid all block movement — the rover just stops and the terminal log tells you what it hit. Check the grid and plan a route around it.
Yes — this is genuine JavaScript, the same language that runs on most websites you use. moveForward(), the loop, all of it would work the same way in a real script.
